section_summary: This section documents a surge of public, church, and humanitarian appeals asking the Roosevelt administration to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, fuel, scrap iron, machinery, credit, and other supplies believed to support Japan’s war in China and its bombing of civilians. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could be invoked only after a presidential finding that a state of war existed, would embargo both China and Japan, and did not authorize controls on ordinary commodities; they also cite export-license totals and condemn the bombing of civilian populations. The section additionally contains internal memoranda, cross-reference sheets, resolutions, petitions, a Red Cross-related response, and cables from Canton reporting continued Japanese bombing.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Henry Stauffer concerning aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and policy basis for continuing to license aircraft and other arms exports during the undeclared war between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both belligerents only if the President proclaimed that a state of war existed. Roosevelt had decided that invoking the act was not in the broad interests of the United States. The letter cites the value of arms-export licenses issued to China and Japan and reiterates Hull’s condemnation of bombing civilians and of its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Mary B. Rhodes letter to the President concerning American supplies for Japan
subfiles.from: Mary B. Rhodes
subfiles.about: Questions whether the United States is furnishing Japan with munitions and other materials used to wage war against China.
subfiles.summary: Rhodes asks whether American exports are enabling Japan to continue the war and the bombing of civilians. She argues that citizens have a right to know where Japan obtains its aircraft and munitions and appeals to the President’s conscience.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mary B. Rhodes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Responds to Rhodes’s protest by outlining the limits of the Neutrality Act and the administration’s policy toward exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply says that a presidential war proclamation would trigger an embargo on arms to both China and Japan, while no current authority allowed an embargo on Japan alone. It adds that the statute did not cover commodities outside the proclaimed arms list. Green cites export-license totals and the Secretary of State’s public opposition to bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: William H. Harrison forwarding letter for Chattanooga Methodist resolutions
subfiles.from: William H. Harrison
subfiles.about: Forwards resolutions adopted by a Chattanooga Methodist gathering and asks Hull to help carry them out.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports that ministers, lay leaders, spouses, and others representing approximately 12,000 Methodists adopted the enclosed resolutions at Centenary Church on June 20. As chairman of the meeting, he asks Hull to use his influence in support of their letter and spirit.

subfiles.title: Chattanooga Methodist resolution on the Sino-Japanese War
subfiles.from: Chattanooga District, Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for measures preventing American governmental or private resources from aiding Japan’s aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution declares that Japan invaded China and that materials purchased in America were contributing to Chinese deaths, suffering, and property loss. It asks the President and Congress to prevent American material and financial resources from directly or indirectly assisting Japan.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to William H. Harrison
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Methodist resolution and explains why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that, without a proclamation, no authority existed to prohibit shipments to Japan alone. The act also did not permit the President or Secretary of State to stop exports of commodities outside the arms list. The response says invocation was judged contrary to American interests and supplies export-license totals for both belligerents.

subfiles.title: O. L. Tanquary letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: O. L. Tanquary
subfiles.about: Asks how extensive American exports of oil, machinery, aircraft equipment, and other raw materials to Japan can continue under American neutrality policy.
subfiles.summary: Tanquary praises Hull’s diplomacy, particularly during the Panay incident, but expresses concern about the volume of supplies leaving Southern California for the belligerents, especially Japan. He asks whether neutrality creates a moral obligation for the federal government to curb such trade.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to O. L. Tanquary
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that existing neutrality legislation did not authorize a unilateral embargo on Japan or restrictions on ordinary commodities.
subfiles.summary: The response distinguishes arms and implements of war from oil, machinery, and other commodities outside the statutory list. It says that a war proclamation would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan and that Roosevelt had decided not to invoke the act. The letter concludes with totals for licensed arms exports to both countries.

subfiles.title: Office of Arms and Munitions Control filing divider
subfiles.from: Department of State, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Serves as a departmental letterhead or filing-divider page between correspondence groups.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the heading of the Department of State’s Office of Arms and Munitions Control. No substantive message, date, or addressee is present.
keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Japanese commercial credits
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Suggests language for answering Ernest A. Tichenor’s reference to a proposed credit pool for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The proposed paragraph explains that international trade is normally financed through commercial banking credits. It states that the Department possessed no information about Japanese borrowing in the United States beyond ordinary commercial accommodations.

subfiles.title: Ernest A. Tichenor letter to the President
subfiles.from: Ernest A. Tichenor
subfiles.about: Protests American war-material shipments and a reported credit pool that could finance continued sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Citing an article in The Witness, Tichenor says Japan’s war against China might have ended without increasing American supplies of war material. He asks Roosevelt to change the situation and help save China for the Chinese.

subfiles.title: Works Progress Administration referral of Tichenor’s letter
subfiles.from: Betty Reasoner, for the Works Progress Administrator
subfiles.about: Forwards Tichenor’s letter after it was mistakenly delivered to the Works Progress Administration.
subfiles.summary: The WPA explains that the June 22 letter was addressed to the President but apparently reached the agency in error. It sends the letter to the State Department without acknowledgment for whatever consideration the Department wishes to give it.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Ernest A. Tichenor
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Tichenor’s concerns about arms exports and a Japanese credit pool.
subfiles.summary: Green repeats that only a presidential finding of war would activate an arms embargo and that it would apply to both China and Japan. The President had determined that invocation was not in the overall American interest. Regarding the credit pool, Green says trade is normally financed by commercial credits and the Department knew of no exceptional Japanese borrowing arrangements.

subfiles.title: Elizabeth Rowen letter protesting war-material exports
subfiles.from: Elizabeth Rowen
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American exports that assist Japan’s military operations against civilian populations.
subfiles.summary: Although heavily degraded by OCR, the letter clearly concerns American war materials sent to Japan and their use against civilians. Rowen frames the issue as one of American responsibility for the brutality of the war.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Elizabeth Rowen
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits on restricting war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that the Neutrality Act could be applied only after a presidential finding of war and would then prohibit arms exports to both sides. Roosevelt had decided that invoking it was not in the broader interests of the United States. Green also cites the monetary value of arms-export licenses issued to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Woodbury letter on humanitarian relief and American responsibility
subfiles.from: Mr. Woodbury
subfiles.about: Argues that humanitarian relief for China is contradicted by continued American exports supporting Japanese attacks.
subfiles.summary: Woodbury compares China’s plight to disasters in India, China, Ohio, and Yokohama that elicited American relief and asks Americans to respond generously again. He then argues that relief alone is morally inconsistent if the government knowingly allows war materials to sustain Japanese bombing of women and children. The letter warns that the American people and government share responsibility if they tolerate such a policy.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mr. Woodbury
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Woodbury’s protest with the administration’s standard explanation of neutrality law and export licensing.
subfiles.summary: The letter says the Neutrality Act would embargo both China and Japan only after a presidential war proclamation and could not presently be used against Japan alone. Roosevelt had concluded that invocation would not serve the broad national interest. The reply also supplies the value of licensed arms exports to each country.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on American aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file concerning the Aeronautical Chamber of Commerce Executive Committee’s position on exporting American planes to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The file note cross-references document 700.00110/378. Its subject is the export of American planes to Japan and the position taken by the Executive Committee of the Aeronautical Chamber of Commerce.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for American Red Cross letter from Davis
subfiles.from: American Red Cross / Davis
subfiles.about: Points to a separately filed Red Cross letter criticizing the contradiction between raising Chinese-relief funds and permitting war supplies to reach Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note directs readers to file 893.48/1597 for the underlying letter. It records the view that Americans considered it foolish to solicit Chinese-relief donations instead of preventing shipments of war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Mr. Davis concerning Chinese-relief fundraising
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Addresses Red Cross difficulties in raising Chinese-relief funds because of the government’s continued licensing of arms exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull regrets that public criticism of export policy is hindering Red Cross fundraising and suggests that chapters explain the legal limits of the Neutrality Act. He reiterates that any embargo would apply to both China and Japan and that Roosevelt had declined to invoke the act. Hull provides updated export-license totals and refers to his June 11 statement opposing sales of aeronautical equipment used to bomb civilians.

subfiles.title: A. J. Fisher telegram reporting the bombing of Canton
subfiles.from: A. J. Fisher, President, American Association, Canton
subfiles.about: Urges immediate American action to stop munitions supplies to Japan amid continued bombing of Canton civilians.
subfiles.summary: Fisher reports that Japanese forces are continuing their merciless bombing of Canton’s civilian population. He says America can prevent suffering by stopping munitions supplied to Japan and conveys the strong appeal of Americans in Canton for Hull’s immediate help.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Consular Officer at Canton concerning Fisher’s telegram
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Canton
subfiles.about: Directs the consular officer to give Fisher the Department’s explanation of neutrality law, export licensing, and opposition to bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses Fisher’s telegram, the 1937 Joint Resolution, and the arms-traffic pamphlet and suggests a detailed response. The proposed language explains that a war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, whereas no authority existed for a Japan-only embargo. It provides export-license figures and points Fisher to Hull’s June 11 condemnation of aerial attacks on civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Calvary Methodist Church resolution and petition against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: Paul G. Hayes and members of Calvary Methodist Church, Minneapolis
subfiles.about: Protests the use of American materials, weapons, aircraft, and credit in Japan’s operations against China and requests all lawful preventive measures.
subfiles.summary: The resolution describes Japan as the aggressor, condemns attacks on undefended cities, noncombatants, missions, and hospitals, and alleges that American materials, bombers, shells, and credits sustain the campaign. The congregation protests profits derived from Japanese aggression and asks the government to prevent American resources from assisting Japan directly or indirectly. Two additional pages contain congregants’ signatures and addresses.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Calvary Methodist resolution and refers Hayes to an earlier departmental reply.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges the July 3 resolution signed by Hayes and members of the Minneapolis congregation. Rather than restating the policy, he calls attention to the Department’s July 13 reply to Hayes’s earlier letter transmitting the same resolution.

subfiles.title: San Francisco mayor’s office letter forwarding Fisher’s cable
subfiles.from: Eric Cullenward, Executive Secretary
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of A. J. Fisher’s cable from Canton to Mayor Angelo J. Rossi.
subfiles.summary: Cullenward sends the State Department, for its information, a copy of the cable received by the Mayor of San Francisco. The enclosed cable concerns Japanese bombing in Canton and American munitions exports.

subfiles.title: A. J. Fisher cable to the Mayor of San Francisco
subfiles.from: A. J. Fisher, President, American Association, Canton
subfiles.about: Appeals to the mayor to help stop American munitions supplies to Japan during the bombing of Canton.
subfiles.summary: The cable reports relentless Japanese bombing of Canton civilians. Fisher says America can prevent suffering by halting munitions supplied to Japan and urges the mayor’s immediate assistance on behalf of Americans in Canton.

subfiles.title: Miss Munger letter concerning supplies exported to Japan
subfiles.from: Miss Munger
subfiles.about: Protests American supplies reaching Japan and requests a change in policy.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten text is severely degraded, but the related reply identifies its subject as exports of supplies to Japan. The correspondent appeals for an effective policy response to the suffering produced by the conflict in China.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Miss Munger
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the government’s limited legal authority over arms and commodity exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential finding of war would trigger a prohibition on arms exports to both China and Japan, but no current authority permitted an embargo against Japan alone. The Joint Resolution did not cover commodities outside the proclaimed arms list. The letter says invocation was not considered in the national interest and supplies export-license totals.

subfiles.title: Mary W. Roe letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Mary W. Roe
subfiles.about: Asks what can be done to stop crude oil, scrap iron, raw cotton, and armaments from reaching aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Roe deplores the destruction of civilian life and property in China. She says she understands that ending American shipments of oil, scrap iron, cotton, and arms could stop the war within months and asks how the flow of the sinews of war can be halted.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mary W. Roe
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Roe’s request for an embargo on oil, scrap iron, cotton, and armaments exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a Neutrality Act proclamation would embargo arms to both sides, while no authority existed for a unilateral embargo on Japan. He emphasizes that the statute did not authorize restrictions on commodities such as oil, scrap iron, and cotton unless they fell within the proclaimed arms list. The President had declined to invoke the act, and the letter gives arms-export license totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: C. P. Weeks letter advocating aid to China
subfiles.from: C. P. Weeks
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to deny weapons to Japan, extend extensive credit and military supplies to China, and defend American treaty interests.
subfiles.summary: Weeks condemns Japanese attacks on Chinese civilians and criticizes the administration for failing to match its statements with action. He advocates unlimited credit and supplies for China, cooperation with England and France, stronger American forces in China, and use of reconstruction work to reduce American unemployment. The letter also warns of Japanese activity near the Pacific Coast and Canada and portrays support for China as both a moral duty and a strategic and commercial opportunity. Weeks encloses a letter from V. K. Wellington Koo.

subfiles.title: V. K. Wellington Koo letter to C. P. Weeks
subfiles.from: V. K. Wellington Koo
subfiles.about: Thanks Weeks for his sympathy and expresses confidence in China’s resistance to Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Koo recalls pleasant memories of Columbia and says letters from former college associates provide comfort and strength. He reports that the Chinese nation supports determined resistance, that civilian and military morale is excellent, and that China remains confident of ultimate victory.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to C. P. Weeks
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains neutrality policy in response to Weeks’s proposals and returns Koo’s enclosed letter.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a declaration that war existed would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan and that ordinary commodities lay outside the Joint Resolution. Roosevelt had determined that invocation would not serve the overall American interest. The reply includes export-license totals and returns the letter from Chinese Ambassador V. K. Wellington Koo as requested.

subfiles.title: Miss Erskine letter protesting shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Miss Erskine
subfiles.about: Urges stronger action against shipments of American fuel, machinery, and other war-supporting materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Erskine condemns Japanese aggression and argues that American materials help sustain its destructive campaign in China. She urges Hull to heed public indignation, even if restricting exports imposes costs on American businesses, and offers support and encouragement for firmer action.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Miss Erskine
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Answers Erskine’s protest by explaining neutrality law, licensed exports, and the administration’s position on civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green says a presidential finding of war would halt arms exports to both China and Japan, while neither a Japan-only embargo nor controls on ordinary commodities were authorized. Roosevelt had decided against invoking the act in the national interest. The letter cites export-license totals and repeats Hull’s June 11 condemnation of bombing civilians and supplying its material means.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping blaming Roosevelt and Hull for continued trade with Japan
subfiles.from: New Salem newspaper
subfiles.about: Claims that Roosevelt and Hull bore responsibility for mass casualties because they failed to prohibit trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The clipping attributes to H. V. Kaltenborn the view that Japan’s invasion of China would have ended had the United States stopped trade. It criticizes Roosevelt’s belated and voluntary approach to bombing-plane sales after thousands of Canton residents had been killed or injured.

subfiles.title: Miss Allen letter enclosing clipping about trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Miss Allen
subfiles.about: Asks whether the clipping’s accusation is true and whether Hull possessed power to stop all trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen asks if Roosevelt and Hull placed the financial interests of a few above worldwide humanitarian sentiment. She specifically requests clarification on whether the Secretary of State had authority to halt all commerce with Japan.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Miss Allen
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Allen’s clipping and questions by outlining the limits of federal power over trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a Neutrality Act proclamation would stop arms exports to both belligerents, not Japan alone. The act did not empower the President or Secretary of State to prohibit ordinary commodity exports, and Roosevelt had determined that invocation was not in the broader national interest. The reply concludes with the value of licensed arms exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: George C. Warren letter concerning bombing planes and munitions
subfiles.from: George C. Warren
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government can stop American sales of bombing planes, bombs, and munitions for the undeclared war without entering the conflict.
subfiles.summary: Warren says that he and millions of other citizens are deeply troubled by reports of American producers selling bombing planes and possibly other munitions to Japan and China. He characterizes the business as nefarious and asks whether it can be ended without bringing the United States into war.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to George C. Warren
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Assistant Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains why the government had not prohibited bombing-plane and war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no current authority allowed restrictions on Japan alone. The President had concluded that invoking the act would not best serve the country as a whole. The letter cites export-license figures and recalls Hull’s public condemnation of bombing civilians and of manufacturers who materially encouraged it.
